opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and I think it's one where a lot of papers actually get it wrong, so let me try to be careful.

The first thing I'd say is that you have to **match the state size**, not just the parameter count. Both sliding-window attention and linear attention are, in a sense, fixed-memory models at inference time. Sliding-window attention keeps a KV cache of the last W tokens, so its memory is roughly W times the head dimension times two, for keys and values. Linear attention keeps a matrix-valued recurrent state, roughly d_k by d_v per head. If you give sliding-window attention a window of 4,096 and compare it against a linear attention model with a tiny state, of course the sliding window wins, but that's not a fair fight. So the cleanest comparison is to hold the recurrent memory footprint constant and ask: given the same number of bytes of state, which way of using that memory is better?

The second thing is that the two make very different trade-offs in *how* they use that memory. Sliding window is lossless but local: it remembers everything perfectly within the window and nothing outside it. Linear attention is lossy but global: in principle it can carry information from arbitrarily far back, but it compresses everything into that fixed state, so you get interference, especially with the vanilla additive update. That's exactly why things like gating and the delta rule matter so much. They give the model a way to forget or overwrite, which makes the compression much more effective. So when you compare, you should also be explicit about *which* linear attention you mean. Comparing sliding window to plain linear attention from 2020 versus to something like Gated DeltaNet gives very different conclusions.

Third, you need to **choose the evaluation carefully**. On standard language modeling perplexity, sliding window is surprisingly strong, because most of the predictive signal in natural text is local. So if you only look at perplexity, you might conclude that you don't need linear attention at all. But once you look at tasks that need long-range retrieval or state tracking, like needle-in-a-haystack, multi-query associative recall, or some reasoning-style tasks where information needs to persist beyond the window, the picture changes. Sliding window just falls off a cliff past its window length, whereas a good linear attention model degrades more gracefully. So a fair comparison should include both short-context quality and genuinely long-context tasks, and ideally report performance as a function of the distance between where information appears and where it's needed.

Fourth, there's the **efficiency side**, and you have to compare at matched wall-clock or matched FLOPs, not just asymptotic complexity. Both are linear in sequence length, but the constants differ a lot. Sliding window can reuse FlashAttention-style kernels and is very hardware-friendly. Linear attention needs chunkwise parallel algorithms to be efficient on GPUs; with good kernels it's competitive, but a naive implementation will look terrible. So if one side has a heavily optimized kernel and the other doesn't, your throughput comparison is really measuring engineering effort.

And finally, I think the most interesting answer in practice is that they're complementary rather than competing. Sliding window is great at precise local recall, linear attention is good at compressing long-range context, so hybrids that combine the two, sometimes with a few global attention layers as well, tend to do better than either alone. But to know *why* the hybrid works, you first need those controlled comparisons: same state size, same training data and tokens, same parameter budget, and a mix of short- and long-context evaluations.

r001.rationale: The response says to hold the recurrent memory footprint constant and compare both methods with the same number of bytes of state, explicitly describing the sliding-window KV cache and linear-attention state.

r002.rationale: It discusses wall-clock time, FLOPs, sequence-length complexity, and kernel efficiency, but does not say that efficiency in memory-bound decoding is governed mainly by how much state must be read from memory.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing is that people often compare them under the wrong axis. Sliding-window attention and linear attention are both ways of getting a constant-size state, so the natural thing to do is to match on state size and then ask which one uses that memory better.

For sliding-window attention, the state is the KV cache for the window. If your window is W tokens and you have d head dimensions, that's roughly 2 times W times d per head. For linear attention, the state is the d by d matrix, or d by d_v if the key and value dimensions differ. So if you want a fair fight, you pick a window size such that the KV cache occupies about the same memory as the linear attention state, and then compare quality and throughput. In practice, with head dimension 128, that means a window on the order of a few hundred tokens, which is actually quite small. A lot of papers that claim sliding-window wins are using windows of 4K or 8K, and at that point you are comparing against a state that is tens of times larger. That's not a comparison of the mechanisms, it's a comparison of memory budgets.

The second axis is what the state can actually represent. Sliding window is lossless but myopic: it remembers the last W tokens exactly and forgets everything before that completely. Linear attention is lossy but has unbounded range: it compresses the entire history into the matrix, so old information is still there, just blurred. Those are very different failure modes. If your benchmark is something like local language modeling or code completion where most of the useful signal is nearby, sliding window will look great. If it's retrieval over a long document, a needle at position 100 with a window of 512 just disappears, while linear attention at least has a chance, especially the gated or delta-rule variants that manage the state better.

So I'd say a fair comparison needs three things. One, match the state size, not the sequence length. Two, use a mix of tasks that probe both recency and long-range recall, because each mechanism has a task family it trivially wins. Three, report wall-clock and memory on the same hardware with properly optimized kernels for both, because for a long time linear attention was judged with naive implementations while sliding window got FlashAttention. Once you have chunkwise parallel kernels for linear attention, the throughput story changes a lot.

And honestly, the conclusion I keep coming back to is that they are complementary rather than competing. Sliding window handles the sharp local precision that linear attention is bad at, and linear attention handles the long-range summary that sliding window physically cannot. Most of the hybrid designs people are converging on now are just that combination, which to me is the real answer to the question.

r001.rationale: It says to match the sliding-window KV cache’s memory to the linear-attention state’s memory, choosing a window size that uses about the same memory.

r002.rationale: The response discusses matching state memory and measuring throughput, but does not explain that memory-bound decoding efficiency is governed mainly by how much state must be read from memory.

astra-6.text:
I’d start by asking what we want to hold fixed. Sliding-window attention keeps a bounded set of recent tokens, while linear attention typically compresses the history into a fixed-size state. So even though both can scale linearly with sequence length, they’re making different trade-offs about what information they retain.

For a controlled comparison, I’d use the same backbone, training data, token budget, and training recipe, and change the attention mechanism. But I’d also give each method a comparable tuning budget, because a configuration that works well for one may be poor for the other.

Then I’d compare quality at matched resource budgets. For example, under the same inference-memory budget, how large a sliding window can you afford, and how large a state can linear attention maintain? At matched latency or training compute, which gives better quality? Matching parameter counts alone doesn’t answer those questions.

I’d measure prefill and decoding separately, on the same hardware, with optimized implementations and several sequence lengths and batch sizes. And I’d test both local modeling and tasks that require information from far back in the context. Linear attention can carry information from the whole history, but that doesn’t mean it preserves every detail; sliding-window attention preserves recent tokens explicitly, but has a limited direct reach.

So I’d want a quality-versus-cost curve, rather than a single number declaring one method the winner.

r001.rationale: The response proposes comparing the largest sliding window and linear-attention state affordable under the same inference-memory budget, which communicates matching their retained state sizes as a fair basis.

r002.rationale: It discusses inference memory and decoding measurements, but does not explain that memory-bound decoding efficiency is governed mainly by how much state must be read from memory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to compare them under the same resource budget, rather than assuming that linear attention is automatically more efficient. Sliding-window attention also has linear complexity in sequence length when the window size is fixed, so the constants and the actual implementation matter a lot.

I would match the model size, training data, and training compute, then compare quality alongside measured throughput, memory usage, and inference latency. For sliding-window attention, you can vary the window size; for linear attention, you can vary the size of its recurrent state. That gives you a quality–efficiency curve instead of one potentially misleading comparison.

And you should test different kinds of tasks. Sliding-window attention preserves detailed access to recent tokens, while linear attention compresses information from the past into a fixed-size state. So local language modeling and long-range retrieval may expose very different strengths. You want to distinguish the benefit of accessing a longer history from the ability to preserve and retrieve precise information from that history.

r001.rationale: The response suggests varying window size and recurrent-state size, but does not propose matching the maximum KV-cache size to the recurrent-state size.

r002.rationale: It recommends measuring memory use and latency, but does not explain that memory-bound decoding efficiency is governed mainly by how much state must be read from memory.
